item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I respect this point of view, and I think there's probably a sizeable chunk of readers who have a similar perspective to the one you've expressed here. For a lot of folks, explaining how a "magic trick" is done spoils the sense of mystery. Sort of a narrative corollary of Clarke's Law: "Sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic." Once a particular "magic" has been explained, it becomes just another kind of science.

However, I don't tend to react that way myself. The solution to one mystery, for me, opens a whole other vista of additional mysteries. I'm fascinated by the various canons people have come up with, the particular rules of each and the tantalizing spots where those rules overlap and synergize. At least once a day I find myself eagerly jotting new questions into my sandbox like "can Karcists obey conservation of mass?" or "how do Mekhanist spiderbot ladies with ceramic facemasks shop for groceries?" Sometimes the answers come from cobbled-together bits of borrowed lore, and sometimes I fill in the blanks with my own imagination.

I don't think there's a wrong way to approach the wiki. It's art, and art is what you like however you like it; it's got room for everyone and then a little more room. But I definitely need to remind myself that different people enjoy the weirdness in different ways. Lots of readers won't want a peek under the chassis when I come up with some preposterous new piece of headcanon. And that's okay.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I…
Don’t like this.
Not because it is badly written, mind you. It’s really good in that regard. I just hate the idea behind it.
Specifically, the idea of a unified magic system for the universe of the foundation.
I know this isn’t the first time such a thing has been proposed, but I am still going to go against it. The SCP universe is special because it has no underlying rules. Things can happen without any massive hidden clockwork determining it.

+ show block
– hide block

Anomalies aren’t kept by the foundation because they they aren’t understood, they are kept because they are anomalies, chinks in the armour of the universe, things that go against the rules. I think the foundation should never find out all there is to know about most scips, at least not in the near future.
I read this site because I want to believe that a moving statue moves not because of magical residue, or due to a reality bender waving their fingers, ir because it’s situation happened to coincide with one of the magical ways of enmagifiying something, but because it wants to.
And the ability to simply slap the word “magic” onto four or five of the strangest, most enigmatic GOIs, in my opinion, simplifies them. What do all these cults want, and why are they willing to do the things they want to do? Magic. What caused the chaos insurgency to become what they are? They wanted magic. It….feels like so much less. And maybe it’s just my head-canon clashing with this, but I liked them more when they weren’t like that.
There are a few smaller things. I just got off of rereading 003, and saw quite a few people getting mad about an author self insert. At the time, it felt unnecessary, and paranoid, but if they posted their arguments here, I’d get their point of view a lot more. You know what you are doing, moose.
Also, the deer ghost thing was pointless. They were all onboard with what the director was saying, throwing a moose at them didn’t feel like it added much, except maybe showing how the director doesn’t really get humour.
Speaking of her, how did a type blue reach the post of site director? Why do her peers trust her with that position, given that whole “losing a part of yourself, the foundation can never do that” speech. Which was awesome, I should add.
Why do the “executioners” have a magic school?
All in all, I do like a lot of this, such as the character herself, the library info, the taskforce… but I’m still sgainst the idea.
-1.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

As a last note, I seem to remember an scp that was a pen and paper style guide that could teach you spells, and it stood out to me since there was no reall drawback to it. Does anyone remember that one? How would that fit into this?

item.content:encoded:
Delayed response, but alchemists would also be considered thaumaturges.

In the umbrella sense, but not in the specific sense. Sort of how I'm "genderqueer", but "genderqueer" is also an umbrella term synonymous with non-binary, which includes things I am not (like "agender").

DrChandra is on-point.

I'll add: Magic is definitely not always ritualistic, but Director Moose (as distinct from me!) tends to emphasize that because the Serpent's Hand does (bunch of book readers, those), and so does she. That's her background. But magic is always subject to various rules (depending on the types of energies used) that reality benders are not subject to.

Director Moose also tends to imply that certain rules are a little more universal than they are, based on her own background and experience and research and expertise.

The biggest general rule is that magic needs to follow a rule-set and draws upon energies theoretically accessible to any human (whether or not in practice this is true at all — for instance, for genetically-based magic that you can't access without being born a certain way).

Reality-bending is changing reality according to nothing but how your own mind works.

Is there a blurry line there in many edge cases? Yes.

The third 'powers' category: Deities or demigods and similar entities also follow a rule-set, but a rule-set that only applies to deities, demigods, and those entities. Their powers are inaccessible to humans. A human could become one of these entities in extreme edge cases, but they wouldn't be human anymore.

Hey, another blurry line between these and reality benders! Especially because from an ordinary human POV, there's no real difference between a reality bender and a god or demigod.

RE: "how does each power manifest?" — in a trillion different ways for each. The GOC figured out a way to detect the types of energy (or byproducts) they generate, but I doubt they work the same way every time.

(I do need to edit the Q&A section and put this into Moose's words, but I'm presently working on another project! This count as a rough draft.)

item.content:encoded:
Thamaturges have blue auras. Reality Bender's have green, and it's interesting that the distinction between these colours isn't always obvious. But in general, the difference is that magic seems to be ritualistic. In order to accomplish a certain goal, you have to recite an incantation or complete a ritual, the difficulty of which is roughly proportional to how powerful the result are. This article also makes mention of the fact that rituals produce a certain kickback that needs to be dealt with.

It's hypothetically possible for anyone to become a Thaumaturge, but few do, just like anyone could hypothetically become a hollywood actor. What separates muggles from mages appears to be ineffable.

Reality Bending is not learned, it is either an innate trait or possibly acquired under bizarre circumstances. Reality Benders don't need spells and rituals, they just think of something and it happens, and they don't have to worry about kickback.

In terms of Elan Vital Energy, Thaumaturges are the same as ordinary humans and are using specific methods to focus their EVE into Aspect Radiation, with rituals having very specific effects.

Reality Benders can produce Aspect Radiation at will, and are limited purely by imagination.

I'll admit, when I saw that this was a thing, I had hope for it. But overall, as an introduction to how magic works in this universe, I find it really disappointing.

For every good thing about this, there's something else that sets it back. The Foundation are opening themselves up to the anomalous community! Oh, wait, they don't officially have type-blues, because that would actually be awesome and make the organization have a sense of levity. Still, unofficially, they have magic! Oh, wait, anyone can do it with enough effort, so it's not that special. The GOC has a school to teach magic! But it's run by the GOC, which have even less levity than the Foundation.

On a final note, I really do not like the fact that there seems to be a trend lately to refer to the Foundation, in-universe, as the "SCP Foundation", even if the person talking is an ex-Serpent's Hand member. It just sounds wrong.

This is a mix of good and bad; some of this, granted, is due to conflicts in headcanons, and I may use some of the information here in later tales. Without the author avatar, it'd get a netural vote. With that, it's pushed into a downvote. It's not the fact that it's a particular author avatar, but AAs in general are a pet peeve of mine.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for your comment — I found it very helpful.

It's vastly more powerful than any other group,
It's like a Mary Sue GoI.

Right, but the Hand/Library is not a GoI. You're falling into the trap that the Serpent's Hand falls into — conflating the Library and the Hand together. The Serpent's Hand wants people to think that, because it sure makes it sound awesome (and puffs up their egos; they are the True Defenders of the Library, which would neverrrr survive without them). Unfortunately for them, this is far from the case. It's the other way around: Without the Library, the Hand would be screwed.

Also, the Library sees the Foundation as a serious, serious threat. The Library is — or at least, the Librarians are — afraid of the Foundation specifically (the GOC they just think are assholes). That's why it doesn't let most of their members in.

I didn't specify that here because…well, I forgot that some people might react that way to reading this, heh.

The Library is also not on Earth. It's most analogous to another planet. It's more powerful than the Foundation only in the sense that the planet Mars is more powerful than the Foundation, due to the difficulty in occupying the planet Mars. (And the Library is afraid the Foundation will eventually figure out how to occupy it.)

You can see the POV of some of the servants of the Library (the Archivists) on the Library site itself here: http://wanderers-library.wikidot.com/thearchivistslog

In this canon/mainstream canon, the Foundation is the most powerful anomalously-related organization on Earth. This stems directly from their (in practice) near-infinite resources. They are 'weak' in only two categories:
(1) They come second only to the GOC in terms of political pull with world governments. (Headcanon, though, that they are number one with regards to the US government, which makes this… less of a weakness. But also explains why they often work with the GOC.)
(2) Outside of Sigma-3 and a few other Task Forces and Thaumiel SCPs, they don't make use of anomalies. And they don't have 'ears on the ground' in the anomalous community. And outside of Sigma-3 they don't have access to the Library (even the GOC has people who can get into the Library who aren't part of the GOC). Plus they have reasons to not indulge too much in Magical Shit (as established in the article). This leads to a pretty large deficiency in knowledge. This is what Sigma-3 exists to shore up.

That said, I understand not liking the magic aspects anyway.

It's entirely likely that I could've done better by portraying magic as much weirder here; my goal was to make it 'in line' with other presentations of magic on the site (Navarro isn't my creation, for example, nor was the Library and such), but that doesn't mean I couldn't have gone further.

I'll keep all this in mind when I edit this article. Although the Magic Stuff is still gonna stay in, of course.

I am really not feeling the whole Serpent's Hand/Wanderer's Library thing. I realize there is no canon, but I do think the mainlist articles hold some degree of extra clout. And the mainlist articles give a pretty clear image of the Foundation as being really, really powerful on a global scale. The Library seems to trivialize all that. It's vastly more powerful than any other group, and the Foundation here is just sort of appeasing it. It's like a Mary Sue GoI.

I'm also not too fond of some of the more powerful depictions of the GOC, and the whole "magic is real" thing in general. I can read about magic in any fantasy novel. I want to see miles long subterranean human arms, toasters that force you to speak about me in the first person, and freaky aquatic piles of human tissue. That's what separates SCP from other scifi/fantasy works.

item.content:encoded:
This is really impressive stuff, I can't imagine the amount of work that went into writing this.

Aside from being incredibly useful and interesting (I'm personally adding all of this new info to my headcanon), this somehow manages, along with this group's other entries in the contest, to legitimize an idea that most site members would have scoffed at in almost any other context - that the Foundation could be working with wizards. I feel like this is the start of something new and different and great, something that will leave a lasting mark on the site.

Two small criticisms:

1. While I appreciate how thorough this is, I think some parts could be pared down a little.

2. This part here:

Sigma-3 are the people whose job it is to know if some cultists are summoning Cthulhu. Generally, their friends and neighbors don't want the world to end. But maybe they can't really do much to stop it.

I know this is meant to foreshadow SCP-2975 - Another Sun, but you're literally describing the exact situation that they're going to run into. I would suggest a subtler approach.

Well done though, +1

Oh, and best line in the article:

Yes, I see you, Agent Navarro, stop waving.

item.content:encoded:
rehashing bits of worldbuilding that we've see elsewhere.

A completely legit critique. While obviously most of this is new (the "another goddamn magic system" was designed to tie in heavily with existing material and leave basically infinite wiggle room, but is still as far as I know completely new), I did deliberately rehash some stuff. Figure I may as well explain my intentions!

This was partially an attempt to fully introduce people to the Library and Library-related elements in a way that not even our Serpent's Hand did. Hence the Library walkthrough which won't be unfamiliar to well-read people (though I added original details and denizens and played up the grandeur aspect, plus showed details that already existed but almost no one knows about if they weren't lucky enough to be an active RPer many years ago).

(full disclosure, our actual original team name was "Wanderers Library Shills" ahahaha. In retrospect we could've emphasized Sigma-3's interaction with other groups more — more material for later!)

Thank you for your comments!
